section: Safety > Warning Symbols and Definitions
text: This manual uses warning symbols to alert you to potential hazards. The Safety alert symbol indicates potential personal injury hazards. Safety messages that follow this symbol must be obeyed to avoid possible injury or death. DANGER indicates a hazardous situation which, if not avoided, will result in death or serious injury. WARNING indicates a hazardous situation which, if not avoided, could result in death or serious injury. CAUTION indicates a hazardous situation which, if not avoided, could result in minor or moderate injury. NOTICE addresses practices not related to personal injury.

section: Safety > General Safety
text: Before use, read and understand the manufacturer's instructions, Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS), employer's safety practices, and ANSI Z49.1. Keep the welder out of reach of children and keep children and bystanders away while operating. Place the welder on a stable location before use; if it falls while plugged in, severe injury, electric shock, or fire may result. Do not overreach and keep proper footing and balance at all times. Stay alert and watch what you are doing. Do not use a welder while tired or under the influence of drugs, alcohol, or medication. Avoid unintentional starting by ensuring you are prepared before turning on the welder. Never leave the welder unattended while energized; turn power off if you have to leave.

section: Safety > Fume and Gas Safety
text: Welding and plasma cutting produce toxic fumes. Exposure to welding exhaust can increase the risk of developing certain cancers including larynx and lung cancer. Additional health risks from welding fume exposure include early onset of Parkinson's disease, heart disease, ulcers, damage to reproductive organs, inflammation of the small intestine or stomach, kidney damage, and respiratory diseases such as emphysema, bronchitis, or pneumonia. Use natural or forced air ventilation and wear a NIOSH-approved respirator to protect against fumes. Do not use the welder near degreasing or painting operations. Keep your head out of fumes and do not breathe exhaust fumes. Use enough ventilation, exhaust at the arc, or both, to keep fumes and gases out of your breathing zone.

section: Safety > Fume and Gas Safety > Confined Areas
text: Work in a confined area only if it is well-ventilated, or while wearing an air-supplied respirator. Have a recognized specialist in Industrial Hygiene or Environmental Services check the operation and air quality and make recommendations for your specific welding situation. Follow OSHA guidelines for Permissible Exposure Limits (PEL's) and the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists recommendations for Threshold Limit Values (TLV's) for fumes and gases.

section: Safety > Arc Ray Safety
text: Arc rays can injure eyes and burn skin. Wear ANSI-approved welding eye protection featuring at least a number 10 shade lens rating. Wear leather leggings, fire-resistant shoes or boots during use. Do not wear pants with cuffs, shirts with open pockets, or any clothing that can catch and hold molten metal or sparks. Keep clothing free of grease, oil, solvents, or any flammable substances. Wear dry, insulating gloves and protective clothing. Wear an approved head covering to protect the head and neck, including aprons, capes, sleeves, shoulder covers, and bibs designed and approved for welding procedures. Wear an approved welding jacket or long sleeves to protect forearms from radiation burns. When welding overhead or in confined spaces, wear flame-resistant ear plugs or ear muffs to keep sparks out of ears.

section: Safety > Electrical Safety
text: Electric shock can kill. Turn off, disconnect power, and discharge the electrode to ground before setting down torch/electrode holder and before service. Do not touch energized electrical parts or wear wet or damaged gloves. Do not touch electrode holder, electrode, welding torch, or welding wire with bare hands. Connect to a grounded, GFCI-protected power supply only. Do not use the welder near water or damp objects. People with pacemakers should consult their physician before use, as electromagnetic fields in close proximity to heart pacemakers could cause pacemaker interference or failure. Do not expose welders to rain or wet conditions, as water entering a welder will increase the risk of electric shock.

section: Safety > Electrical Safety > Cord Management
text: Do not abuse the power cord. Never use the cord for carrying, pulling, or unplugging the welder. Keep the cord away from heat, oil, sharp edges, or moving parts. Damaged or entangled cords increase the risk of electric shock. Do not use the welder outdoors. Insulate yourself from the workpiece and ground. Use nonflammable, dry insulating material if possible, or use dry rubber mats, dry wood or plywood, or other dry insulating material large enough to cover your full area of contact with the work or ground. The welding machine must be connected to the power source in accordance with applicable electrical codes.

section: Safety > Fire Safety
text: Arc and slag can cause fire. Clear away or protect flammable objects. Remove or make safe all combustible materials for a radius of 35 feet (10 meters) around the work area. Use fire-resistant material to cover or block all open doorways, windows, cracks, and other openings. Keep an ABC-type fire extinguisher near the work area and know how to use it. Maintain a safe working environment by keeping the work area well lit with adequate surrounding workspace, free of obstructions, grease, oil, trash, and other debris. Do not operate welders in atmospheres containing dangerously reactive or flammable liquids, gases, vapors, or dust. Provide adequate ventilation in work areas to prevent accumulation of such substances.

section: Safety > Fire Safety > Fire Watch
text: If working on a metal wall, ceiling, etc., prevent ignition of combustibles on the other side by moving the combustibles to a safe location. If relocation of combustibles is not possible, designate someone to serve as a fire watch, equipped with a fire extinguisher, during the welding process and for at least one half hour after the welding is completed. Do not weld or cut on materials having a combustible coating or combustible internal structure without an approved method for eliminating the hazard. Do not dispose of hot slag in containers holding combustible materials. After welding, make a thorough examination for evidence of fire and be aware that visible smoke or flame may not be present for some time after the fire has started.

section: Safety > Fire Safety > Pressurized Containers
text: Do not apply heat to a container that has held an unknown substance or a combustible material whose contents, when heated, can produce flammable or explosive vapors. Clean and purge containers before applying heat. Vent closed containers, including castings, before preheating, welding, or cutting.

section: Safety > Welder Use and Care
text: Do not use the welder if the switch does not turn it on and off. Any welder that cannot be controlled with the switch is dangerous and must be repaired. Disconnect the plug from the power source before making any adjustments, changing accessories, or storing the welder. Such preventive safety measures reduce the risk of starting the welder accidentally. Prevent unintentional starting by ensuring the switch is in the off-position before connecting to power source or moving the welder. Carrying or energizing welders that have the switch on invites accidents. Store idle welders out of the reach of children and do not allow persons unfamiliar with the welder or instructions to operate it. Use the welder and accessories in accordance with instructions, taking into account working conditions and the work to be performed. Do not use the welder for pipe thawing.

section: Safety > Maintenance
text: Maintain the welder by checking for misalignment or binding of moving parts, breakage of parts, and any other condition that may affect the welder's operation. If damaged, have the welder repaired before use, as many accidents are caused by poorly maintained welders. Have your welder serviced by a qualified repair person using only identical replacement parts to ensure the welder's safety is maintained. Maintain labels and nameplates on the welder, as they carry important information. If unreadable or missing, contact Harbor Freight Tools for a replacement. Unplug the welder from its electrical outlet before any inspection, maintenance, or cleaning procedures.

section: Safety > Gas Shielded Welding - Cylinder Safety
text: Cylinders can explode when damaged. Do not weld on a pressurized or closed cylinder. Do not allow an electrode holder, electrode, welding torch, or welding wire to touch the cylinder. Keep cylinders away from any electrical circuits, including welding circuits. Keep protective cap in place over the valve except when the cylinder is in use. Use only correct gas shielding equipment designed specifically for the type of welding you will do and maintain this equipment properly. Protect gas cylinders from heat, being struck, physical damage, slag, flames, sparks, and arcs. Use proper procedures to move cylinders.

section: Safety > Symbology
text: The manual uses various symbols to indicate important information: Wire Feed (Speed), Workpiece Ground Cable, Torch Cable, Overheat Shutdown Indicator, Cooling Fan, Housing Ground Point. Technical abbreviations include: VAC (Volts Alternating Current), A (Amperes), OCV (Open Circuit Voltage), KVA (Kilovolt Amperes = Volts / 1000 * Amperes), IPM (Inches Per Minute), AWG (American Wire Gauge). Hazard symbols indicate: Electric Shock Hazard (do not touch energized parts), Inhalation Hazard (keep head out of fumes and use proper ventilation), Fire Hazard (keep flammable materials away during welding), Arc Ray Hazard (wear welding helmet with properly rated filter lens), and Pacemaker Hazard (welding processes may interfere with pacemakers).

section: Safety > Grounding
text: To prevent electric shock and death from incorrect grounding wire connection, check with a qualified electrician if you are in doubt about whether the outlet is properly grounded. Do not use the welder if the power cord or plug is damaged; have it repaired by a service facility before use. The green wire inside the cord is connected to the grounding system in the welder. The green wire must be the only wire connected to the welder's grounding system and must never be attached to an electrically live terminal. Never leave the grounding wire disconnected or modify the power cord plug in any way. Make sure the tool is connected to an outlet having the same configuration as the plug.

section: Safety > Extension and Replacement Cords
text: Do not use an extension cord on this welder. Use only one of the supplied power cords for this welder or an identical replacement cord. Do not install a thinner or longer cord on this welder. Do not patch cords of any length together for this item, as patches may allow moisture to penetrate the insulation, resulting in electric shock. If the tool must be reconnected for use on a different type of electric circuit, the reconnection should be made by qualified service personnel, and the tool should comply with all local codes and ordinances after reconnection.

text: MIG welding specifications for the Vulcan OmniPro 220. Power input options: 120 VAC / 60 Hz or 240 VAC / 60 Hz. Current input at output: 20.8 A at 100 A (120V) or 25.5 A at 200 A (240V). Wire speed: 50-500 IPM. Wire spool capacity: up to 12 lb spool.

Welding current range: 10 A-125 A (120V) or 10 A-175 A (240V). Rated duty cycles: 40% @ 125 A with 100% @ 90 A (120V) or 30% @ 175 A with 100% @ 105 A (240V). section: Controls > Front Panel Controls
text: The Vulcan OmniPro 220 front panel includes the following controls and connections: Wire feed power cable input, Power switch (on/off), LCD display screen for settings and diagnostics, Right knob for adjusting material thickness and voltage/torch control, Left knob for setting wire diameter/rod diameter/electrode diameter and adjusting feed speed/amperage, Main control knob for selecting process and navigating menus, Home button for returning to main screen, Back button for returning to previous screen, Spool gun gas outlet (for optional spool gun), MIG gun/spool gun cable socket, Negative socket for ground clamp or TIG torch cable, Positive socket for wire feed or electrode holder cable, and storage compartment. Note: When using an optional spool gun (sold separately), connect the spool gun gas hose to the spool gun gas outlet.

section: Controls > Interior Controls
text: Inside the welder door are several mechanical controls: Cold wire feed switch for manually feeding wire during setup, idler arm (spring-loaded) that can be moved to apply tension to the wire, wire feed mechanism that drives the welding wire, wire spool where the welding wire is loaded, spool knob for securing large wire spools, feed tensioner knob for adjusting wire feed pressure, wire inlet liner that guides the wire into the feed mechanism, feed roller knob for accessing and changing the feed roller, wire feed control socket (internal connection), and foot pedal socket (inside welder) for optional TIG foot pedal connection.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Wire Spool Installation
text: Before proceeding with wire spool installation, turn the power switch off and unplug the welder. Remove the protective foam and cardboard from the welder before setup. For 1-2 pound wire spool installation: Pull up on the door latch to open the door. Remove the wingnut and spacer. If replacing a spool, remove the old spool and all remaining wire from the liners. Place the new wire spool over the spool spindle and against the spool brake pad. To prevent wire feed problems, set the spool so that it will unwind clockwise. Replace the spacer over the spool spindle and secure the spool in place with the wingnut. Important: If the wire spool can spin freely, the wingnut is too loose. This will cause the welding wire to unravel and unspool which can cause tangling and feeding problems.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Wire Spool Installation > 10-12 lb Spools
text: For 10-12 pound wire spool installation: Remove the wingnut and spacer. If replacing a spool, remove the old spool and all remaining wire from the liners. Place the spool adapter over the spool spindle and against the spool brake pad. Place the new wire spool over the adapter and line up the pin on the adapter with the hole in the spool. To prevent wire feed problems, set the spool so that it will unwind clockwise. Replace the spacer over the spool spindle and secure the spool in place with the wingnut. Important: If the wire spool can spin freely, the wingnut is too loose. This will cause the welding wire to unravel and unspool which can cause tangling and feeding problems. Screw the spool knob into the spool adapter. Turn the feed tensioner knob counterclockwise to loosen it enough to pull it down and remove tension. The spring-loaded idler arm will move up as shown.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Feed Roller Instructions
text: Check that the feed roller is correct for the type of wire being used (solid core or flux-cored) and that it is turned to properly match the wire size marked on the wire spool. Unscrew the feed roller knob counterclockwise. Remove the feed roller knob to expose the feed roller. Flip or replace the feed roller as needed and confirm that it is the correct roller for the type of wire being used and that the number showing is the same as the wire diameter on the spool. Screw the feed roller knob back into place to secure the feed roller. The feed roller has two sides: solid core side with V-groove channels for 0.025" and 0.030"/0.035", and flux-cored side with knurled groove channels for 0.030"/0.035" and 0.045".

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Gun Cable and Wire Feed Setup
text: Loosen the knob on the wire feed mechanism, then insert the gun cable connector through the hole on the welder front and into the socket on the wire feed. Ensure that the gun cable connector is fully inserted into the socket on the wire feed mechanism as shown. If the connector is not fully inserted, the gas connection will leak, preventing shielding gas from reaching the welding arc. Do not overtighten the knob to prevent damage. Insert the wire feed control cable through the hole on the welder front and connect it to the wire feed control socket inside the machine, then tighten the lock ring on the cable plug. Note that the plug on the cable fits into the socket in one specific orientation only.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Polarity Setup
text: For DCEN (Direct Current Electrode Negative) polarity setup used for flux-cored (gasless) welding: Plug the ground clamp cable into the positive (+) socket. Plug the wire feed power cable into the negative (-) socket. Twist cables clockwise all the way to lock in place. For DCEP (Direct Current Electrode Positive) polarity setup used for solid core (gas shielded) welding: Plug the ground clamp cable into the negative (-) socket. Plug the wire feed power cable into the positive (+) socket. Twist cables clockwise all the way to lock in place.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Gas Cylinder Setup
text: For solid core (gas shielded) MIG welding, determine which type of shielding gas would be appropriate for the welding you will do by referring to the settings chart on the inside of the welder door. With assistance, set the gas cylinder (not included) onto a cabinet or cart near the welder and secure it with two straps (not included) to prevent tipping. Remove the cylinder's cap. Stand to the side of the valve opening, then open the valve briefly to blow dust and dirt from the valve opening, then close the cylinder valve. Locate the regulator (included) and close its valve until it is loose, then thread the regulator onto the cylinder and wrench-tighten the connection. When using C100 shielding gas, connect the enclosed CGA 580/320 adapter to the inlet connection of the regulator and wrench-tighten. Attach the gas hose (included) to the regulator's outlet and the welder's gas inlet, wrench-tightening both connections.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Wire Loading and Tension
text: Securely hold onto the end of the welding wire and keep tension on it during wire loading. If this is not done, the welding wire will unravel and unspool which can cause tangling and feeding problems. Cut off all bent and crimped wire. The cut end must have no burrs or sharp edges; cut again if needed. Keep tension on the wire and guide at least 12 inches of wire into the wire inlet liner and feed guide. Make sure the welding wire is resting in the groove of the feed roller, then push the wire idler arm down and swing the feed tensioner up to latch it across the tip of the arm. After the wire is held by the tensioner, you may release it. The tension should be 3-5 for solid wire and 2-3 for flux-cored wire. Too much force on flux-cored wire will crush it and may cause feeding issues. Stainless steel wire is less flexible than other welding wire, so keep the gun cable straight while feeding stainless steel wire.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Cold Wire Feed Testing
text: Plug either 120 VAC or 240 VAC power cord into power input socket (plug will only fit one way). Do not touch the gun's trigger. Plug the power cord into a properly grounded, GFCI-protected 120 VAC (20 amp rated) or 240 VAC receptacle that matches the plug and turn the power switch ON. The circuit must be equipped with delayed action-type circuit breaker or fuses. Point the gun away from all objects. Press and hold the cold wire feed switch until the wire feeds through two inches. The wire liner may come out with the welding wire; this is normal, just push the wire liner back into the gun. If the wire does not feed properly and the spool is stationary, turn OFF and unplug the welder and slightly tighten the feed tensioner clockwise before retrying.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Wire Drive Tension Check
text: To check the wire's drive tension, press and hold the trigger to feed the wire against a piece of wood from 2 to 3 inches away. After pressing the trigger, the wire will stop feeding after 3 seconds if there is no arc. Check tension for less than 3 seconds. If the wire stops instead of bending, unplug the welder, slightly tighten the feed tensioner clockwise, and try again. If the wire bends from the feed pressure, then the tension is set properly. Before proceeding, turn OFF the power switch and unplug the power cord from its electrical outlet. Turn OFF the power switch and unplug the power cord from its electrical outlet. Close the door and make sure it is securely latched.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Nozzle and Contact Tip Installation
text: Select a contact tip that is compatible with the welding wire used. Slide the contact tip over the wire and thread it clockwise into the MIG gun, then tighten the contact tip. Replace the nozzle and cut the wire off at 1/2" from the tip to achieve the correct 1/2" stickout (contact tip to work distance).

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Optional Spool Gun Setup
text: To set up the optional spool gun (sold separately), plug the ground clamp cable into the negative (-) socket and plug the wire feed power cable into the positive (+) socket. Twist cables clockwise all the way to lock in place. Loosen the knob on the wire feed mechanism, then insert the spool gun cable connector through the hole on the welder front and into the socket on the wire feed. Ensure that the cable connector is fully inserted and tighten the knob securely. If the connector is not fully inserted, the gas connection will leak, preventing shielding gas from reaching the welding arc. Do not overtighten the knob to prevent damage. Insert the wire feed control cable through the hole on the welder front and connect to the wire feed control socket inside the machine, then tighten the lock ring on the cable plug. Connect the gas hose on the spool gun cable connector to the spool gun gas outlet on the front of the welder. Refer to gas setup procedures for further shielding gas setup information. Refer to the spool gun manual for operational information.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Basic Wire Welding Overview
text: Flux-cored wire welding is used to weld mild steel and stainless steel without shielding gas. MIG welding uses solid wire and shielding gas, and is used to weld mild steel and stainless steel. MIG welding can also be used to weld thinner workpieces than flux-cored welding can. Aluminum welding can be performed with an optional spool gun (sold separately) using aluminum wire and shielding gas. Good welding takes a degree of skill and experience. Practice a few sample welds on scrap before welding your first project. Additional practice periods are recommended whenever you weld a different thickness of material, a different type of material, a different type of connection, or using a different process. Make practice welds on pieces of scrap to practice technique before welding anything of value. Protective gear must be worn when using the welder including minimum shade number 10 full face shield or welding mask, ear protection, welding gloves, sleeves and apron, NIOSH-approved respirator, and fire-resistant work clothes without pockets.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Setting Up The Weld
text: Make practice welds on pieces of scrap the same thickness as your intended workpiece to practice technique before welding anything of value. Clean the weld surfaces thoroughly with a wire brush or angle grinder; there must be no rust, paint, oil, or other materials on the weld surfaces, only bare metal. Use clamps (not included) to hold the workpieces in position so that you can concentrate on proper welding technique. The distance (if any) between the two workpieces must be controlled properly to allow the weld to hold both sides securely while allowing the weld to penetrate fully into the joint. The edges of thicker workpieces may need to be chamfered (or beveled) to allow proper weld penetration. When welding equipment on a vehicle, disconnect the vehicle battery power from both the positive connection and the ground before welding to prevent damage to some vehicle electrical systems. Clamp the ground cable to bare metal on the workpiece near the weld area, or to metal work bench where the workpiece is clamped.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Duty Cycle
text: Avoid damage to the welder by not welding for more than the prescribed duty cycle time. The duty cycle defines the number of minutes, within a 10 minute period, during which a given welder can produce a particular welding current without overheating. For example, a welder with a 40% duty cycle at 100 A welding current must be allowed to rest for at least 6 minutes after every 4 minutes of continuous welding. Failure to carefully observe duty cycle limitations can easily over-stress a welder's power generation system contributing to premature welder failure. The welder has an internal thermal protection system to help prevent this sort of over-stress. When the welder overheats, it automatically shuts down and a warning screen appears in the LCD display window. The welder automatically returns to service after cooling off. Should this occur, rest the MIG gun on an electrically non-conductive, heat-proof surface such as a concrete slab, well clear of the ground clamp, and allow the welder to cool with the power switch on so that the internal fan will help cool the welder.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Rated Duty Cycle Chart
text: Rated duty cycle for MIG welding at 120 VAC: 100% continuous use at 75 A, or 40% use at 100 A for 10 continuous minutes (4 minutes welding / 6 minutes resting). Rated duty cycle for MIG welding at 240 VAC: 100% continuous use at 115 A, or 25% use at 200 A for 10 continuous minutes (2-1/2 minutes welding / 7-1/2 minutes resting). When normal operation resumes, use shorter welding periods and longer rest periods to prevent needless wear.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Settings Setup
text: Press the home button on the control panel. Turn the main control knob until the desired process appears on the LCD display screen. Press the main control knob to select the process. Note: Press main control knob to go to next screen. Press back button to return to the previous screen. Adjust settings for the selected process. For polarity and gas settings: Plug cables in according to screen. Connect gas according to screen. Set SCFH between 20-30 for MIG welding. For wire diameter and material thickness: Turn left knob to set wire diameter. Turn right knob to set material thickness.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Auto Weld Settings
text: The Vulcan OmniPro 220 is a synergic welder that automatically computes recommended amperage and voltage based on wire diameter and material thickness inputs. For auto weld settings: Turn left knob to adjust wire feed speed (amperage). Turn right knob to adjust voltage. If the wire feed speed or voltage settings are adjusted manually, the white mark on the line shows the recommended setting for your wire/electrode diameter and workpiece thickness. This visual indicator helps you optimize settings around the machine's recommended point.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Optional Settings
text: Press the main control knob to enter optional settings. Turn the main control knob until desired setting appears on screen. Press the main control knob to select desired setting. Turn the main control knob to adjust the setting. Available optional settings include: Run-In WFS - Adjust wire speed before it contacts workpiece. This setting represents a % of the pre-set wire feed speed (WFS). Inductance - Adjust length of arc. Increase for more fluid puddle and flatter bead. Decrease for colder puddle. Spot Timer - Set timer for spot welding. Recall Setting - Retrieve saved settings. Save Setting - Program up to 5 different configurations. Turn main control knob to scroll between 5 available slots. Press main control knob to access OVERWRITE MEMORY SETTING screen and turn main control knob to choose YES selection. Press main control knob to save current welder settings. Note: The initial settings may need to be adjusted after stopping and carefully inspecting the weld. Proper welding takes experience.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Gas Shielded Solid-Core Wire
text: For gas shielded solid-core wire MIG welding, open the gas cylinder valve all the way. Set the flow gauge to the SCFH value indicated on the settings chart. Important safety note: Do not open gas without proper ventilation. Fix gas leaks immediately. Shielding gas can displace air and cause rapid loss of consciousness and death. Shielding gas without carbon dioxide can be even more hazardous because asphyxiation can start without feeling shortness of breath.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Basic Welding Technique
text: Press and hold the trigger and contact the area to be welded with electrode wire to ignite arc. For a narrow weld, you can usually draw the wire in a steady straight line. This is called a stringer bead. For a wider weld, draw the wire back and forth across the joint. This is called a weave bead and takes practice to perform properly. Direct the welding wire straight into the joint. This gives an angle of 90 degrees (straight up and down) for butt (end to end) welds, and an angle of 45 degrees for fillet (T-shaped) welds. The contact tip should remain within 1/2" of the work surface. This distance is called CTWD - Contact Tip to Work Distance.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > MIG Gun Angles
text: For MIG welding using solid wire and shielding gas, the end of the MIG gun should be tilted so that the wire is angled anywhere in-between straight on and 15 degrees away from the direction you are welding. The amount of tilt is called the push angle. When using flux-cored wire without shielding gas, the end of the MIG gun should be tilted so that the wire is angled anywhere in-between straight on and 15 degrees in the direction you are welding. The amount of tilt is called the drag angle.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > After Practice Welding
text: After welding a test weld on a piece of scrap for a few seconds, stop and check your progress. Clean, then compare your weld's appearance with the diagrams and descriptions in the welding tips section. After making any necessary adjustments, continue to weld while carefully following the duty cycle guidelines. If the welder is used too long, a warning screen appears in the LCD display window and the unit automatically shuts down. The welder automatically returns to service after cooling off. Should this occur, rest the MIG gun on an electrically non-conductive, heat-proof surface such as a concrete slab, away from the ground clamp. Allow the welder to cool with the power switch on so that the internal fan will help cool the welder. When welding is complete, set the MIG gun down on a heat-proof, electrically non-conductive surface. Turn the power switch OFF. Allow the welder to cool down, then unplug the power cord.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Cleanup and Storage
text: Remove the ground clamp from the workpiece or table and disconnect the MIG gun. Respool wire by clipping wire, removing gas nozzle/contact tip on MIG gun, releasing idler arm on wire feed mechanism, and rotating the wire spool counterclockwise. Be sure to securely hold wire as it is being respooled because the end of wire has a tendency to quickly unravel once it clears the wire feeder. For MIG welding only: Close the shielding gas cylinder valve securely. Remove regulator and replace cap. Disconnect gas hose from welder. Store and secure gas cylinder.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Setup - Connect Cables
text: For TIG welding setup, plug the ground clamp cable into the positive socket and twist clockwise all the way to lock in place. Plug the TIG torch cable (TIG torch sold separately) into the negative socket and twist clockwise all the way to lock in place. Insert the foot pedal cable (foot pedal sold separately) through the hole on the welder front and connect to the foot pedal socket inside the machine. Secure by turning the collar clockwise until tight. For connecting the shielding gas hose, refer to the connect shielding gas section on the next page.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Shielding Gas Setup
text: With assistance, place a 100% argon cylinder (not included) onto a cabinet or cart near the welder and secure it in place with two straps (not included) to prevent tipping. Remove the cylinder's cap. Stand to the side of the valve opening, then open the valve briefly to blow dust and dirt from the valve opening. Close the cylinder valve. Locate the regulator (included) and close its valve until it is loose, then thread the regulator onto the cylinder and wrench-tighten the connection. Connect the shielding gas hose on the TIG torch cable connector to the regulator's outlet and wrench-tighten the connection.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Power Cord Connection
text: Plug either 120 VAC or 240 VAC power cord into the power input socket. Note that the plug will only fit one way. Important warning: Do not plug the cord into the wall outlet at this time.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Sharpen Tungsten Electrode
text: To avoid electrode contamination, dedicate a fine grit grinding wheel exclusively to electrode grinding. Important safety warning: Some electrodes may have materials added to them that are hazardous to breathe. Wear a respirator and ANSI-approved safety goggles when grinding an electrode. Shut off the welder and wait until the electrode and torch have cooled enough to handle. Remove back cap. Pull the electrode from the front of the torch (pulling it from rear will damage the collet and create burrs on the electrode). If the electrode has dulled or been otherwise contaminated, use pliers or a suitable tool to grip the electrode above the contaminated section and snap off the end of the electrode. Lightly press the electrode tip against the surface of the grinding wheel at an angle. Rotate the electrode tip until a blunt point is formed. The conical portion of the ideal tip will be 2-1/2 times as long as the electrode diameter. Re-insert the electrode into the collet with the tip protruding 1/8"-1/4" beyond the ceramic nozzle, then re-tighten the back cap.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Assemble TIG Torch
text: Consult the settings chart on top of the welder to determine the proper tungsten electrode size to be used with the thickness of material to be welded. Match collet and collet body sizes to the tungsten electrode size. Thread the collet body into the front of the torch. Make sure the ceramic nozzle size is appropriate for the application. Thread the ceramic nozzle onto the collet body. Insert the collet into the back of the torch and into the collet body. Insert the tungsten electrode into the collet on the front of the torch. Lock the electrode in place with the back cap. The electrode should protrude 1/8" to 1/4" beyond the ceramic nozzle.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Setup - Connect Cables
text: For stick welding setup, plug the ground clamp cable into the negative socket and twist clockwise all the way to lock in place. Plug the electrode holder cable into the positive socket and twist clockwise all the way to lock in place.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Basic TIG / Stick Welding Overview
text: DC TIG welding is used to weld mild steel and stainless steel using a TIG rod and shielding gas. AC TIG welding is used to weld aluminum using a TIG rod and shielding gas. Stick welding is used to weld mild steel and stainless steel using a stick electrode without shielding gas. Good welding takes a degree of skill and experience. Practice a few sample welds on scrap before welding your first project. Additional practice periods are recommended whenever you weld a different thickness of material, a different type of material, a different type of connection, or using a different process. Make practice welds on pieces of scrap to practice technique before welding anything of value. Protective gear must be worn when using the welder including minimum shade number 10 full face shield or welding mask, ear protection, welding gloves, sleeves and apron, NIOSH-approved respirator, and fire-resistant work clothes without pockets. Light from the arc can cause permanent damage to the eyes and skin. Do not breathe arc fumes.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Duty Cycle - TIG
text: TIG welder rated duty cycles for 120 VAC: 40% use at 125 A or 100% continuous use at 90 A for 10 continuous minutes (4 minutes welding / 6 minutes resting). TIG welder rated duty cycles for 240 VAC: 30% use at 175 A or 100% continuous use at 105 A for 10 continuous minutes (approximately 3 minutes welding / 7 minutes resting). Avoid damage to the welder by not welding for more than the prescribed duty cycle time. The duty cycle defines the number of minutes, within a 10 minute period, during which a given welder can produce a particular welding current without overheating. Failure to carefully observe duty cycle limitations can easily over-stress a welder's power generation system.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Duty Cycle - Stick
text: Stick welder rated duty cycles for 120 VAC: 40% use at 125 A or 100% continuous use at 90 A for 10 continuous minutes (4 minutes welding / 6 minutes resting). Stick welder rated duty cycles for 240 VAC: 30% use at 175 A or 100% continuous use at 105 A for 10 continuous minutes (3 minutes welding / 7 minutes resting). This welder has an internal thermal protection system to help prevent over-stress. When the welder overheats, it automatically shuts down and a warning screen appears in the LCD display window. The welder automatically returns to service after cooling off. When normal operation resumes, use shorter welding periods and longer rest periods to prevent needless wear.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Welding Process Setup
text: Turn the power switch to the OFF position, then plug the welder into a properly grounded, GFCI-protected 120 VAC (20 amp rated) outlet or 240 V outlet. The circuit must be equipped with delayed action-type circuit breaker or fuses. Set the TIG torch down on a nonconductive, nonflammable surface away from any grounded objects. Turn the power switch ON. Press the home button on the control panel. Turn the main control knob until the TIG process appears on the LCD display screen. Press the main control knob to select the TIG process. Note: Press main control knob to go to next screen. Press back button to return to the previous screen.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Welding Settings
text: Adjust settings for the TIG process. For polarity and gas settings: Plug cables in according to screen. Connect gas according to screen. Set SCFH between 10-25 for TIG welding. For rod diameter and material thickness: Turn left knob to set rod diameter. Turn right knob to set material thickness. For auto weld settings: Turn left knob to adjust output amperage. Turn right knob to ON to energize TIG torch. Warning: Welder is now energized and open circuit voltage is present.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Optional Settings
text: Press the main control knob to enter optional settings. Turn the main control knob until the desired setting appears on screen. Press the main control knob to select desired setting. Turn the main control knob to adjust the setting. Available optional settings: Recall Setting - Retrieve saved settings. Save Setting - Program up to 5 different configurations. Note: The initial settings may need to be adjusted after stopping and carefully inspecting the weld. Proper welding takes experience.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Arc Initiation and Technique
text: Hold the TIG torch in one gloved hand and the TIG rod (sold separately) in the other gloved hand. Maintain a constant distance between the tungsten electrode and the workpiece: between 1 and 1.5 times the diameter of the electrode. Open the valve on the TIG torch to start gas flow. To initiate the welding arc, push the foot pedal and touch the electrode to the work piece and lift. If not using a foot pedal, touch the electrode to the work piece and lift. When the welding puddle is hot enough, tilt the torch backward about 10-15 degrees from vertical and move it back slightly. Add TIG rod material as needed to the front end of the weld puddle. Alternate between pushing the torch/weld puddle and adding TIG rod material. Important note: Remove the TIG rod each time the electrode is advanced, but do not remove it from the gas shield. This prevents oxidation from contaminating the weld.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Weld Completion and Cleanup
text: When finished welding, release the foot pedal but keep the torch on the weld puddle until the weld solidifies. If not using a foot pedal, pull the torch away from the work piece until the welding arc is broken, then return the gas coverage until the weld solidifies. Close the valve on the TIG torch and turn the right knob to OFF to turn off power to the TIG torch. Set the TIG torch down on a nonconductive, nonflammable surface away from any grounded objects. Turn the power switch OFF. To prevent accidents, after use: Allow the welder to cool down. Unplug the welder's power cord from the outlet. Remove the ground clamp from the workpiece or table. Disconnect TIG torch, ground, and foot pedal cables. Close the gas cylinder's valve securely, remove regulator and replace cap. Disconnect gas hose from welder. Store and secure gas cylinder. Clean, then store welder and its accessories indoors out of children's reach.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Welding Process Setup
text: Turn the power switch to the OFF position, then plug the welder into a properly grounded, GFCI-protected 120 VAC (20 amp rated) outlet or 240 V outlet. The circuit must be equipped with delayed action-type circuit breaker or fuses. Set the electrode holder down on a nonconductive, nonflammable surface away from any grounded objects. Turn the power switch ON. Press the home button on the control panel. Turn the main control knob until the Stick process appears on the LCD display screen. Press the main control knob to select the STICK process. Note: Press main control knob to go to next screen. Press back button to return to the previous screen.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Welding Settings
text: Adjust settings for the STICK process. For polarity setting: Plug cables in according to screen. For electrode type: Turn main control knob to set electrode type. For electrode diameter and material thickness: Turn left knob to set electrode diameter. Turn right knob to set material thickness. For auto weld settings: Turn left knob to adjust output amperage. Turn right knob to ON to energize electrode holder. Warning: Welder is now energized and open circuit voltage is present. The LCD display will show Hot Start and Arc Force optional settings available.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Optional Settings
text: Press the main control knob to enter optional settings. Turn the main control knob until the desired setting appears on screen. Press the main control knob to select desired setting. Turn the main control knob to adjust the setting. Available optional settings: Hot Start - Adjust amperage at start of weld. Arc Force - Adjust weld penetration and smoothness. Recall Setting - Retrieve saved settings. Save Setting - Program up to 5 different configurations. Note: The initial settings may need to be adjusted after stopping and carefully inspecting the weld. Proper welding takes experience.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Arc Ignition and Technique
text: Place the bare metal end of the stick electrode (sold separately) inside the jaws of the electrode holder. Stroke the workpiece lightly to ignite the arc. Tips for igniting the arc: Tap the surface with the electrode, stroke the surface with the electrode, or strike the surface like a match with the electrode. After the arc ignites: Lift the electrode off the workpiece the same distance as the diameter of the bare metal end. Tilt the electrode back 10 to 20 degrees. Drag the electrode to the back end of the weld puddle to deposit material as needed. After practice welding on scrap, stop and check your progress. Perform the strike test according to the strike test procedure on page 34. After making any necessary adjustments, continue to weld while carefully following the duty cycle guidelines.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Weld Completion and Cleanup
text: When finished welding, lift the electrode from the workpiece, then set the electrode holder down on a nonconductive, nonflammable surface away from any grounded objects. Turn the power switch OFF. To prevent accidents, after use: Allow the welder to cool down. Unplug the welder's power cord from the outlet. Remove the ground clamp. Disconnect the electrode holder and ground cables. Clean, then store the welder and its accessories indoors out of children's reach.

section: Welding Tips > Strike Test
text: A test weld on a piece of scrap can be tested by using the strike test procedure. Important safety warning: Wear ANSI-approved safety goggles during this procedure. This test will damage the weld it is performed on. This test is only an indicator of weld technique and is not intended to test working welds. After two scraps have been welded together and the weld has cooled, clamp one scrap in a sturdy vise. Stay clear from underneath while you strike the opposite scrap with a heavy hammer, preferably a dead-blow hammer. A good weld will deform but not break. A poor weld will be brittle and snap at the weld.

section: Welding Tips > Cleaning the Weld
text: Important safety warning: Continue to wear ANSI-approved safety goggles and protective wear when cleaning a weld. Sparks or chips may fly when cleaning. A weld from flux-cored wire welding or stick welding will be covered by slag. Use a chipping hammer to knock this off. Be careful not to damage the weld or base material. Use a wire brush to further clean the weld or use an angle grinder (sold separately) to shape the weld.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld Diagnosis - Penetration
text: Proper penetration: The weld is visible underneath and bulges slightly on top. This represents ideal heat for the workpiece thickness. Inadequate penetration: The weld does not penetrate the joint fully, just on the surface. This indicates the workpiece is not hot enough. Excess penetration or burn-through: Weld droops on top and underneath, or falls through entirely, making a hole. This indicates the workpiece is too hot. To increase workpiece heat and increase penetration (for welding thicker workpieces): Increase weld current, decrease travel speed, use faster wire feed, or use shorter CTWD. To reduce workpiece heat and limit penetration (for welding thinner workpieces): Decrease weld current, increase travel speed, use slower wire feed, or use longer CTWD.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld Penetration Solutions
text: Workpiece overheating causes excess penetration: Reduce wire feed speed, decrease weld current. Travel speed too slow causes excess penetration: Increase travel speed and ensure that travel speed is kept steady. Excessive material at weld causes excess penetration: Reduce wire feed speed. Insufficient weld heat causes inadequate penetration: Reduce travel speed, increase weld current. Workpieces too thick/close causes inadequate penetration: Bevel thick workpieces, allow slight gap, and weld in several passes. Insufficient weld material causes inadequate penetration: Increase wire feed speed. Incorrect welding technique causes inadequate penetration: Maintain 1/2" or less CTWD, keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle, hold MIG gun at proper angles.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld - Not Adhering Properly
text: Weld not adhering properly occurs when gaps are present between the weld and previous bead or between the weld and workpiece. Incorrect welding technique causes this: Place stringer bead at correct place in joint. Adjust workpiece position or weld angle to permit proper welding to bottom of piece. Pause briefly at sides during weave bead. Keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle. Hold MIG gun at proper angles. Insufficient weld heat causes non-adhesion: Increase current, increase wire feed speed. Dirty workpiece causes non-adhesion: Clean workpiece down to bare metal. Insufficient weld material causes non-adhesion: Increase wire feed speed. Workpiece gap too narrow causes non-adhesion: Widen groove or increase bevel.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld - Bend at Joint
text: Bend at joint in wire welds can be caused by improper clamping or excessive heat. For improper clamping: Clamp workpieces securely, make tack welds to hold workpieces. For excessive heat: Weld a small portion and allow to cool before proceeding, increase travel speed, reduce wire feed speed.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld - Coat of Slag
text: Slag is a necessary part of a flux-cored wire weld. It shields the weld from impurities. Clean off the slag with a chipping hammer and wire brush after welding. Gas-shielded MIG welds are protected by the shielding gas and do not need slag to protect them.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld - Burn-Through
text: Wire weld burn-through occurs when base material melts away, leaving a hole in the weld. Workpiece overheating causes burn-through: Reduce current and/or wire feed speed. Travel speed too slow causes burn-through: Increase travel speed and ensure that travel speed is kept steady. Excessive material at weld causes burn-through: Reduce wire feed speed.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld - Crooked/Wavy Bead
text: Wire weld crooked or wavy bead defects are caused by inaccurate welding or inconsistent travel speed. Inaccurate welding causes this: Use two hands or rest hand on steady surface. Inconsistent travel speed causes this: Maintain steady travel speed. CTWD too long causes this: Reduce CTWD.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld - Porosity
text: Wire weld porosity consists of small cavities or holes in the bead. Incorrect polarity: Check that polarity is set correctly for the type of welding. Insufficient shielding gas (MIG only): Increase flow of gas, clean nozzle, maintain proper CTWD. Incorrect shielding gas (MIG only): Use shielding gas recommended by wire supplier. Dirty workpiece or welding wire: Clean workpiece down to bare metal. Make certain that wire is clean and free from oil, coatings, and other residues. Inconsistent travel speed: Maintain steady travel speed. CTWD too long: Reduce CTWD.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld - Excessive Spatter
text: Wire weld excessive spatter defects occur when fine spatter is normal but spatter that is grainy and large is a problem. Dirty workpiece or welding wire: Clean workpiece down to bare metal. Make certain that wire is clean and free from oil, coatings, and other residues. Incorrect polarity: Check that polarity is set correctly for the type of welding. Insufficient shielding gas (MIG only): Increase flow of gas, clean nozzle, maintain proper CTWD. Wire feeding too fast: Reduce wire feed speed. CTWD too long: Reduce CTWD.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld Diagnosis - Penetration
text: Stick weld proper penetration: The weld is visible underneath and bulges slightly on top. This represents ideal heat. Stick weld inadequate penetration: The weld does not contact the joint fully, just on the surface. This indicates insufficient heat. Stick weld excess penetration or burn-through: The weld droops on top and underneath, or falls through entirely, making a hole. This indicates excessive heat. To increase workpiece heat for thicker workpieces: Increase current, weld more slowly. To reduce workpiece heat for thinner workpieces: Decrease current, weld more quickly.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld Penetration Solutions
text: For excess penetration or burn-through in stick welds: Workpiece overheating requires reducing current. Welding speed too slow requires increasing welding speed and ensuring it is kept steady. For inadequate penetration in stick welds: Incorrect welding technique - keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle, hold torch at proper angles. Insufficient weld heat - slow down so fill material has time to melt into the weld location, increase current. Workpieces too thick/close - bevel thick workpieces, allow slight gap, and weld in several passes. Insufficient weld material - increase amount of fill material.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld - Not Adhering Properly
text: Stick weld not adhering properly occurs when gaps are present between the weld and previous bead or between the weld and workpiece. Incorrect welding technique: Place stringer bead at correct place in joint. Adjust workpiece position or weld angle to permit proper welding to bottom of piece. Keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle. Hold electrode and fill material at proper angles. Insufficient weld heat: Increase current. Dirty workpiece: Clean workpiece down to bare metal. Insufficient weld material: Increase amount of fill material. Distance between workpieces too large: Decrease distance and increase bevel.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld - Bend at Joint
text: Stick weld bend at joint is caused by improper clamping or excessive heat. For improper clamping: Clamp workpieces securely, make tack welds to hold workpieces. For excessive heat: Weld a small portion and allow to cool before proceeding, increase weld speed.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld - Coat of Slag
text: Slag is a necessary part of a stick weld. It shields the weld from impurities. Clean off the slag with the chipping hammer and wire brush after welding.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld - Porosity
text: Stick weld porosity consists of small cavities or holes in the bead. Dirty workpiece or fill material: Clean workpiece down to bare metal. Make certain that fill material and electrode are clean and free from oil, coatings, and other residues. Inconsistent welding speed: Maintain steady weld speed.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld - Crooked/Wavy Bead
text: Stick weld crooked or wavy bead defects are caused by inaccurate welding or inconsistent welding speed. Inaccurate welding: Use two hands or rest hand on steady surface. Inconsistent welding speed: Maintain steady weld speed.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld - Excessive Spatter
text: Stick weld excessive spatter occurs when fine spatter is normal but spatter that is grainy and large is a problem. Dirty workpiece or fill material: Clean workpiece down to bare metal. Make certain that fill material and electrode are clean and free from oil, coatings, and other residues.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld - Burn-Through
text: Stick weld burn-through occurs when base material melts away, leaving a hole in the weld. Workpiece overheating: Reduce current. Welding speed too slow: Increase welding speed and ensure that welding speed is kept steady. Excessive material at weld: Reduce amount of fill material.

section: Maintenance > Before Each Use Inspection
text: Before each use, inspect the general condition of the welder. Check for loose hardware, misalignment or binding of moving parts, damaged cord / electrical wiring, frayed or damaged cables, cracked or broken parts, and any other condition that may affect its safe operation. Periodically, have a qualified technician remove the rear panel and use compressed air to blow out all dust from the interior. After every use, store in a clean and dry location. For optimal MIG / Flux-Cored wire weld quality, clean and inspect the MIG gun contact tip and nozzle before each use. Important safety warning: Unplug the welder, rest the tool on a heat-proof, electrically non-conductive surface, and allow all parts of the welder to cool thoroughly before service.

section: Maintenance > MIG Gun Nozzle and Contact Tip Cleaning
text: Make sure that the entire MIG gun is completely cool and that the power cord is unplugged from the electrical outlet before proceeding. Pull the nozzle to remove it. Scrub the interior of the nozzle clean with a wire brush. Examine the end of the nozzle. The end should be flat and even. If the end is uneven, chipped, melted, cracked, or otherwise damaged, the nozzle will adversely affect the weld and should be replaced. Unscrew the contact tip counterclockwise and slide it off the welding wire to remove. Scrub the outside of the tip clean with a wire brush. Clean out the inside of the tip with a tip cleaner (sold separately). Check that the tip is the proper type for the wire size used. Examine the shape of the hole at the end of the contact tip. It should be an even circle and should not be oblong or have any bulges in it. If any problems are noted, replace the contact tip. Select a new tip of the correct size for the welding wire used. Reinstall the tip and securely reinstall the nozzle as well.

section: Maintenance > Replacing the LCD Screen Cover
text: To replace the LCD screen cover: Carefully pry the frame off of the display by inserting a flathead screwdriver (sold separately) into one of the side slots. Insert a new screen cover into the screen frame with the gap facing downward. Insert the frame back into the slot on the display with the top end being placed in first.
