section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Flux-Cored Gasless Polarity
text: DCEN (Direct Current Electrode Negative) polarity is used for flux-cored wire welding without shielding gas. The negative polarity setup ensures that the electrode (welding wire) is negative while the workpiece ground is positive. This configuration is essential for flux-cored wire because the flux coating on the wire itself provides the shielding protection. Using DCEN polarity with flux-cored wire provides better penetration and arc stability for gasless welding operations.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > MIG Gas Shielded Polarity
text: DCEP (Direct Current Electrode Positive) polarity is used for solid core MIG welding with shielding gas. The positive polarity setup ensures that the electrode (welding wire) is positive while the workpiece ground is negative. This configuration is required for MIG welding because the shielding gas provides the arc protection and the positive electrode polarity ensures proper wire feeding and arc characteristics for solid core wire. Always verify cable connections match the specific gas type and wire being used.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Duty Cycle 120VAC
text: MIG duty cycle at 120 VAC power input shows two operational modes: For 100% continuous use at 75 A: You can weld indefinitely without rest breaks at this amperage level. For 40% use at 100 A: You must limit welding to 4 minutes of continuous operation within any 10-minute period, then rest for 6 minutes. Always monitor the internal thermal protection system which will shut down the welder if overheating occurs. Use shorter welding periods and longer rest periods as a general practice to extend equipment life.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Duty Cycle 240VAC
text: MIG duty cycle at 240 VAC power input shows two operational modes: For 100% continuous use at 115 A: You can weld indefinitely without rest breaks at this amperage level, providing increased capacity compared to 120V operation. For 25% use at 200 A: You must limit welding to 2.5 minutes of continuous operation within any 10-minute period, then rest for 7.5 minutes when using maximum amperage. The 240 VAC connection provides higher power capability but requires stricter duty cycle adherence at maximum current settings.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Gas Flow Settings
text: TIG welding gas flow rate is set between 10-25 SCFH (Standard Cubic Feet per Hour) as shown in the settings chart. The specific SCFH value selected depends on the material thickness and welding conditions shown on the inside of the welder door. Proper gas flow is critical for TIG welding to maintain a clean arc and prevent oxidation of the tungsten electrode and weld puddle. Insufficient gas flow can result in porosity, discoloration, and contaminated welds. Excessive gas flow wastes shielding gas and creates turbulent gas patterns that may draw in room air.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > MIG Gas Flow Settings
text: MIG welding gas flow rate is set between 20-30 SCFH (Standard Cubic Feet per Hour) as indicated in the settings chart on the inside of the welder door. For solid core MIG welding with shielding gas, proper gas flow is essential to exclude atmospheric gases from the arc and weld puddle. The specific SCFH value within the 20-30 range depends on nozzle size, gun angle, and travel speed. Check that the MIG gun cable connector is fully inserted into the wire feed mechanism with no O-Rings exposed, as this affects gas delivery to the nozzle.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Duty Cycle 120VAC
text: TIG duty cycle at 120 VAC shows: For 100% continuous use at 90 A: You can weld indefinitely at this amperage without mandatory rest periods. For 40% use at 125 A: You must limit welding to 4 minutes within any 10-minute period, then rest for 6 minutes when using higher amperage. These ratings assume proper ventilation and normal ambient temperature conditions. Monitor for thermal shutdown warnings which indicate the welder needs cooling time.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Duty Cycle 240VAC
text: TIG duty cycle at 240 VAC shows: For 100% continuous use at 105 A: You can weld indefinitely at this amperage, providing higher continuous current capability than 120V operation. For 30% use at 175 A: You must limit welding to approximately 3 minutes within any 10-minute period, then rest for 7 minutes when using maximum amperage. The 240 VAC input provides significantly more power for TIG welding but requires careful duty cycle management at higher amperages.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Duty Cycle 120VAC
text: Stick duty cycle at 120 VAC shows: For 100% continuous use at 90 A: You can weld indefinitely at this amperage without mandatory rest periods. For 40% use at 125 A: You must limit welding to 4 minutes within any 10-minute period, then rest for 6 minutes when using higher amperage. Stick welding creates the most heat of the three processes, so careful attention to thermal limits is important to prevent overheating.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Duty Cycle 240VAC
text: Stick duty cycle at 240 VAC shows: For 100% continuous use at 105 A: You can weld indefinitely at this amperage. For 30% use at 175 A: You must limit welding to approximately 3 minutes within any 10-minute period, then rest for 7 minutes when using maximum amperage. The 240 VAC connection enables higher amperages for stick welding but requires strict duty cycle adherence to prevent thermal shutdown.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > CTWD Control
text: Contact Tip to Work Distance (CTWD) is critical to MIG welding success. The contact tip should remain within 1/2" (0.5 inches) of the work surface. If CTWD is too long, the wire may not feed properly and the arc becomes unstable. A CTWD that is too short can cause spatter and poor weld appearance. Maintaining consistent 1/2" CTWD requires keeping a steady hand and practicing to develop muscle memory. For flux-cored wire without gas, maintaining proper CTWD also ensures adequate shielding from the flux coating.

section: Welding Tips > Example Wire Weld Diagrams
text: Example wire weld diagrams show how to recognize and correct common problems. Good weld shows proper bead profile with even coverage. Voltage too low or wire feed too slow creates a narrow, high bead with poor fusion. Voltage too high or wire feed too fast creates a flat, wide bead with possible porosity. Travel speed too fast creates a thin bead with inadequate fusion. Travel speed too slow creates an excessively large bead with possible burn-through on thin material. CTWD too long or wrong polarity causes unstable arc and poor weld appearance. These visual references help you diagnose weld quality issues.

section: Welding Tips > Example Stick Weld Diagrams
text: Example stick weld diagrams show how to recognize and correct common problems. Clean welds first before inspecting because slag covers the weld. Good weld shows proper bead profile visible under slag. Current too low creates a weak, narrow bead with poor penetration. Current too high creates excessive spatter and poor bead appearance. Weld speed too fast creates a narrow, thin bead with inadequate fusion. Weld speed too slow creates an excessively large bead with possible burn-through. Arc length too short causes difficult arc maintenance. Arc length too long causes unstable arc and poor weld quality. These visual references help you diagnose stick weld quality issues.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Stainless Steel Wire Setup
text: Stainless steel wire is less flexible than mild steel or aluminum welding wire. This reduced flexibility makes it more difficult to feed through the gun cable liner. It is especially important to keep the MIG gun cable straight while feeding stainless steel wire to prevent the wire from buckling or jamming in the liner. Use the cold wire feed function to carefully feed the wire with the gun cable laid out in a straight line. If the wire stops during stainless steel wire feeding, check for kinks in the cable and verify that the feed tensioner is properly set for the wire diameter used.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Electrode Spacing
text: In TIG welding, maintaining a constant distance between the tungsten electrode and the workpiece is critical to arc stability and weld quality. The recommended spacing is between 1 and 1.5 times the diameter of the tungsten electrode. For example, with a 1/16" electrode, maintain a gap of 1/16" to 3/32" from the workpiece. This gap maintains proper arc length and gas shield coverage while preventing tungsten contamination of the weld puddle. Too close spacing risks electrode contact with the puddle; too large a gap can cause erratic arc behavior.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Rod Feeding Technique
text: When adding TIG rod material to the weld puddle, follow proper technique to prevent oxidation and contamination. Always remove the TIG rod each time the electrode is advanced into the puddle material, but keep the rod inside the gas shield at all times. This practice prevents the tungsten electrode and rod from oxidizing in the air between passes. Add rod material to the front edge of the weld puddle where it melts readily. Alternate between advancing the torch (moving the puddle forward) and adding rod material to develop smooth, consistent bead profile.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Electrode Angle
text: Proper stick electrode angle is essential to good weld penetration and bead appearance. After striking the arc, tilt the electrode back 10 to 20 degrees from vertical to maintain proper arc length and puddle control. This slight backward tilt is called the drag angle because you drag the electrode back to deposit material. The electrode should maintain this angle as you move along the joint. Changing the angle during welding creates inconsistent arc length and can result in poor weld quality.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Arc Striking Techniques
text: There are three primary techniques for striking an arc with stick electrodes: Tap the surface with the electrode point briefly, then lift slightly to establish the arc. Stroke the surface with the electrode like striking a match. Strike the surface firmly like starting a match. The stroke technique is often preferred because it provides the smoothest arc initiation. Practice all three methods to develop the technique that works best for you. Each electrode type may respond slightly differently, so test on scrap material before starting your project.

section: Welding Tips > Strike Test Interpretation
text: The strike test is a mechanical test to evaluate weld quality by testing weld ductility rather than strength. A good weld will deform when struck with a hammer but will not crack or break. This indicates that the weld metal and base metal have proper fusion and the material retained its ductility. A poor weld will be brittle and snap or crack at the weld, indicating inadequate penetration, porosity, or other defects. This test damages the weld it is performed on, so only use it on practice welds or test coupons, never on structural parts.

section: Welding Tips > Wire Weld Defect Examples
text: Common wire weld defects visible in cross-section include: Voltage too low or wire feed too slow creates a narrow, high profile with possible porosity. Voltage too high or wire feed too fast creates a flat, wide profile that spreads excessively. Travel speed too fast creates a thin bead that doesn't fill the joint properly. Travel speed too slow creates an overly large bead that wastes material and can cause burn-through on thin material. CTWD too long creates a wavy, unstable bead. Wrong polarity (DCEN for MIG, DCEP for flux-cored) prevents proper arc characteristics.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Gas Regulator Setup
text: The gas regulator included with the Vulcan OmniPro 220 controls the pressure and flow rate of shielding gas to the MIG gun. Before connecting to the cylinder, close the regulator valve until it is loose (turn counterclockwise). After the regulator is threaded onto the cylinder, open the main cylinder valve all the way to ensure full pressure reaches the regulator. Then adjust the flow gauge to the SCFH value indicated on the settings chart for your specific welding process and material. Always stand to the side when opening the cylinder valve briefly to blow dust from the valve before using.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Shielding Gas Type
text: TIG welding requires 100% argon shielding gas for most applications. Argon is an inert gas that provides excellent arc stability and weld quality for mild steel, stainless steel, and other materials. The gas cylinder (not included with the welder) must be secured in place with two straps to prevent tipping during use. Argon is heavier than air and flows easily through the gas delivery system. The purity of argon is important - use welding-grade argon, not industrial-grade, to ensure clean welds without contamination.

section: Specifications > Wire Sizes Available
text: The Vulcan OmniPro 220 can use solid core MIG wire in diameters: 0.025", 0.030", and 0.035". Flux-cored wire is available in: 0.030", 0.035", and 0.045". Each wire diameter has a specific feed roller groove that must be selected before welding. Smaller diameter wire (0.025"-0.030") is suitable for thinner materials and precise work. Larger diameter wire (0.035"-0.045") provides faster deposition rates for thicker materials and production welding. Wire diameter also affects wire speed settings and penetration characteristics.

section: Specifications > Wire Speed and Spool Capacity
text: Wire speed range for the Vulcan OmniPro 220 is 50-500 IPM (inches per minute). This wide range accommodates different wire diameters and materials. Smaller diameter wire typically runs faster (higher IPM) than larger diameter wire. The wire spool capacity is up to 12 lb, accommodating standard MIG wire spools. The wire feeder uses an idler arm and feed tensioner to precisely control wire feed pressure, which is critical for smooth arc operation.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Feed Roller Selection
text: Selecting the correct feed roller is critical to consistent wire feeding. The feed roller has two sides: Solid core side features V-groove channels. Flux-cored side features knurled groove channels. For solid core wire, use the V-groove side with the groove size matching the wire diameter (0.025", 0.030"/0.035" grooves). For flux-cored wire, use the knurled groove side with the groove size matching the wire diameter (0.030"/0.035" or 0.045" grooves). Always check that the number showing on the roller matches the wire diameter on the spool label before starting to weld.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Practice Requirements
text: Good welding requires skill and experience that can only be developed through practice. Always practice several sample welds on scrap material before welding on your actual project. Use scrap material of the same thickness as your intended workpiece to practice technique. Make multiple passes to develop consistent technique before starting valuable work. Additional practice is recommended whenever you work with different material thickness, different material type, different connection type (butt vs fillet), or different welding process.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Ground Clamp Connection
text: The ground clamp must be connected to bare metal on the workpiece near the weld area or to the metal work bench where the workpiece is clamped. Never attempt to weld through the ground clamp - this prevents proper current flow and creates poor weld quality. Clean the ground clamp connection point down to bare metal by scraping away any paint, rust, or oxidation. A clean metal-to-metal contact is essential for proper current flow throughout the welding circuit. The ground clamp cable should be as short as possible to minimize electrical resistance.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Workpiece Surface Preparation
text: Before welding, clean the weld surfaces thoroughly to bare metal using a wire brush or angle grinder. There must be no rust, paint, oil, or other materials on the weld surfaces - only clean bare metal. Poor surface preparation is one of the most common causes of weak welds and porosity. The distance (if any) between the two workpieces must be controlled properly to allow the weld to hold both sides securely while allowing the weld to penetrate fully into the joint. The edges of thicker workpieces (over 1/4") may need to be chamfered or beveled to allow proper weld penetration through multiple passes.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Stringer vs Weave Beads
text: Two basic bead patterns are used in MIG welding: Stringer bead (straight) is used for narrow welds where you draw the wire in a steady straight line along the joint. This creates a narrow, high bead profile with good penetration. Weave bead is used for wider welds where you draw the wire back and forth across the joint in a weaving motion. This creates a wider, flatter bead profile to fill wider gaps. Weave beads take practice to perform properly - the key is maintaining consistent traverse speed and gun angle while moving side to side. For most work, stringer beads are easier and provide better penetration.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Joint Types and Gun Angles
text: Two common joint types require different gun angles: Butt (end-to-end) welds require 90-degree gun angle, pointing straight up and down into the joint. This ensures proper fusion and penetration when joining two pieces edge-to-edge. Fillet (T-shaped) welds require 45-degree gun angle, pointing at the corner where two surfaces meet. This angle allows the weld to properly fill the corner and create a triangular fillet profile. Proper gun angle is critical to weld quality, penetration, and appearance.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Push Angle vs Drag Angle
text: Gun angle terminology varies depending on the process and gas type: Push angle (0-15 degrees) is used with solid core wire and shielding gas. The gun is tilted away from the direction of travel, which pushes the molten metal into the joint. This provides better gas shield coverage and cleaner welds. Drag angle (0-15 degrees) is used with flux-cored wire without shielding gas. The gun is tilted toward the direction of travel, which drags the flux shield behind the arc. This maintains the flux protection as the electrode moves along the joint. Using the wrong angle with the wrong wire type produces poor weld quality.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Thermal Shutdown Warning
text: When the welder overheats due to excessive duty cycle, a warning screen appears in the LCD display window and the unit automatically shuts down to protect internal components. Do not attempt to restart the welder immediately. Set the MIG gun down on a heat-proof, electrically non-conductive surface like a concrete slab, well clear of the ground clamp. Allow the welder to cool with the power switch ON so that the internal cooling fan operates. The welder will automatically return to service after cooling. To prevent thermal shutdown, use shorter welding periods and longer rest periods than the minimum duty cycle specifications.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Torch Setup and Safety
text: The TIG torch must be set down on a nonconductive, nonflammable surface away from any grounded objects whenever the operator is not holding it. The torch carries open circuit voltage when the welder is powered on, so proper placement prevents accidental contact and electrical hazards. Place the torch on a concrete slab or other non-conductive surface. Never leave the torch resting on conductive materials like metal or wet surfaces. Some torches include a valve on the gas line that must be opened manually before striking the arc.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Foot Pedal Operation
text: TIG welding can be controlled with or without a foot pedal (sold separately). With foot pedal: Push the foot pedal to start the arc, vary foot pressure to increase/decrease amperage during welding, release the foot pedal to stop welding. Without foot pedal: Touch the electrode to the workpiece and lift to strike the arc. To adjust amperage without a pedal, you must adjust the amperage setting before starting the arc, then turn the right knob OFF to stop welding. The foot pedal provides superior control for beginners and professionals because it allows real-time amperage adjustment during welding.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > TIG Puddle Control and Technique
text: When the welding puddle is hot enough, tilt the torch backward about 10-15 degrees from vertical and move it back slightly. This backward tilt allows you to see the puddle and control its size. Add TIG rod material as needed to the front end of the weld puddle where it melts readily. Alternate between pushing the torch forward (advancing the puddle along the joint) and adding rod material. This alternating motion creates an overlapping pattern that produces consistent weld strength and appearance. The rod should remain inside the gas shield at all times to prevent oxidation.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Electrode Holder Setup
text: The stick electrode holder must be connected to the positive (+) socket for stick welding when following the standard DCEP polarity setup. The ground clamp must be connected to the negative (-) socket. The electrode holder should be set down on a nonconductive, nonflammable surface away from any grounded objects whenever the operator is not holding it. The holder carries open circuit voltage when the welder is powered on. Hold the electrode holder in a comfortable grip that allows for precise electrode angle control during welding.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Stick Electrode Types
text: Stick welding uses different electrode types for different materials and applications. The LCD display allows you to select the electrode type before welding. Different electrode types have different characteristics including: Arc characteristics (easy-start, smooth, or explosive), Penetration depth (shallow, medium, or deep), Deposition rate (fast or slow), Slag type (heavy or light), and Base metal compatibility (mild steel, stainless, etc.). Always use electrodes appropriate for the material you are welding. Match the electrode diameter to the material thickness - thicker material requires larger diameter electrodes.

section: Welding Tips > Inadequate Penetration - Root Causes
text: Inadequate wire weld penetration occurs when the weld does not penetrate the joint fully but only sits on the surface. Root causes include: Insufficient weld heat (reduce travel speed, increase current), Incorrect welding technique (maintain 1/2" or less CTWD, keep arc on leading edge), Workpieces too thick or gap too small (bevel thick pieces, allow slight gap between pieces), Insufficient weld material deposited (increase wire feed speed). All of these causes can be corrected by adjusting settings and technique before the next weld attempt.

section: Welding Tips > Excessive Spatter Reduction
text: Fine spatter is normal in MIG welding and cannot be completely eliminated, but excessive spatter that is grainy and large indicates a problem. Causes of excessive spatter include: Dirty workpiece or wire (clean to bare metal), Incorrect polarity (DCEP for MIG, DCEN for flux-cored), Insufficient shielding gas flow (increase SCFH, clean nozzle, maintain proper CTWD), Wire feeding too fast (reduce wire speed), CTWD too long (maintain 1/2" or less). Reducing spatter improves weld appearance and reduces cleanup time.

section: Welding Tips > Porosity Causes and Prevention
text: Porosity (small cavities or holes in the weld bead) indicates contamination or insufficient shielding. Prevention includes: Correct polarity (DCEP for MIG, DCEN for flux-cored), Sufficient shielding gas flow (20-30 SCFH for MIG, 10-25 SCFH for TIG), Clean nozzle free of spatter, Proper CTWD (less than 1/2"), Clean workpiece and wire (no oil, dust, or oxidation), Steady travel speed (avoid speed variations). Porosity weakens the weld and should be avoided through proper setup and technique.

section: Welding Tips > Stick Weld Appearance Assessment
text: Stick welds will have a coat of slag over them until cleaned. Always clean the slag off before assessing weld quality. Use a chipping hammer to knock off the slag coating carefully without damaging the underlying weld. Then use a wire brush for further cleaning. Only after slag is removed can you properly see the weld bead profile and assess whether penetration is adequate, appearance is good, and no defects are visible. Clean welds reveal weld quality for proper inspection.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Safe Welder Operation
text: Keep the MIG gun tip clear of grounded objects whenever the welder is plugged in and turned on. Never leave the welder unattended while energized. If you must leave the work area, turn the power switch OFF and unplug the welder from the outlet. Do not touch the gun trigger while feeding wire through during setup. Parts of the welder including the MIG gun tip may be at welding voltage, presenting an electric shock hazard. Always treat the welder with respect and follow all electrical safety precautions.

section: Maintenance > Periodic Professional Maintenance
text: Periodically have a qualified technician remove the rear panel and use compressed air to blow out all dust from the welder interior. This dust removal is important because dust accumulation can impair cooling efficiency and lead to thermal shutdown. The frequency of professional maintenance depends on welding frequency and environment - daily use in dusty conditions may require monthly maintenance, while occasional hobby use might need annual maintenance. Maintain labels and nameplates on the welder as they carry important information about specifications and safety.

section: Maintenance > Storage and Off-Season Care
text: After every use, store the welder in a clean and dry location. Do not store outdoors or in damp environments as moisture can cause rust and electrical failures. Allow the welder to cool completely before storing. Store accessories like wire spools, gas cylinders, and cables in a clean, dry place as well. For long-term storage (more than a month), consider removing the wire spool and replacing it when you restart welding. Periodically check stored welders for signs of rust or damage before returning them to service.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Inductance Adjustment
text: Inductance adjustment is an optional setting that controls the arc length and puddle fluidity. Increase inductance for: More fluid puddle behavior, Flatter bead profile, Better appearance. Decrease inductance for: Colder puddle for thinner material, Tighter arc control. Inductance doesn't change the overall weld energy but affects how the energy is delivered to the arc. Experimentation with inductance can help optimize weld appearance and handling for specific applications.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Run-In WFS Setting
text: Run-In Wire Feed Speed (WFS) is an optional setting that controls wire speed before it contacts the workpiece. This setting is represented as a percentage of the pre-set wire feed speed. For example, 50% run-in speed means the wire feeds at half the normal speed before arc ignition, then speeds up to the set value when the trigger is pulled. Run-In WFS helps smooth arc initiation and reduces spatter at the start of the weld. Higher run-in percentages create smoother starts but slower arc pickup.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Spot Timer Setting
text: Spot Timer is an optional setting for spot welding - joining two pieces at a single point without continuous beads. When spot timer is activated and you press the trigger, the welder automatically stops after a set time period. This allows consistent spot weld size without manually releasing the trigger. Spot welding is commonly used in automotive repair and sheet metal fabrication. Set the timer value based on the material thickness and desired weld nugget size.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Hot Start Setting
text: Hot Start is an optional setting in stick welding that adjusts the amperage at the moment of arc initiation. Higher hot start values create a more forceful arc start that helps ignite the arc and establish a stable arc quickly. Lower hot start values create a gentler arc start useful for thin materials or electrodes that are sensitive to high initial current. Most operators benefit from moderate hot start settings that provide reliable arc initiation without excessive spatter.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Arc Force Setting
text: Arc Force is an optional setting in stick welding that adjusts weld penetration and smoothness. Increasing arc force provides: Deeper penetration, More forceful arc action, Better tie-in at edges. Decreasing arc force provides: Smoother, quieter arc, Less spatter, Better control for thin materials. Arc force doesn't change the base amperage but adds extra current boost when the electrode touches the puddle. Proper arc force setting is important for operator comfort and weld quality.

section: TIG / Stick Welding > Save and Recall Settings
text: Both TIG and Stick processes allow you to save up to 5 different configurations to memory. To save settings: Access Optional Settings menu, select Save Setting, turn main control knob to scroll between the 5 available slots, press main control knob to access the OVERWRITE MEMORY SETTING screen, turn main control knob to choose YES, press main control knob to save the current settings. To recall saved settings: Select Recall Setting from the Optional Settings menu. This feature is useful when working with multiple material thicknesses or electrode types in a single work session.

section: MIG / Flux-Cored Wire Welding > Save and Recall Settings
text: MIG welding also allows you to save up to 5 different configurations to memory for different wire diameters, thicknesses, or projects. Access the Optional Settings menu after adjusting your initial wire diameter and material thickness settings. Save settings that work well for your common applications to quickly recall them later. This feature reduces setup time and improves consistency when switching between different projects or materials throughout the day.
